This is not sufficiently precise. And I suspect making this a "should" instead of a "must" is unintentional.

A good model is https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#nonce-attributes:concept-element-attributes-change-ext . Things to fix while converting it into that algorithmic format:

- "valid value" is undefined. You should talk about the attribute's state, e.g. "if _oldValue_ was in the X state and _value_ is in the Y state".

Or you can use named parameters per https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#algorithm-declaration, but that requires more work at both the call and declaration sites. (An example of something in HTML that uses named parameters is https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#navigate , if you want to go that route.)

When a pop-up is closed/hidden, we support animations for it, like making it fade out. During this closing animation, we attach event listeners to the animations to run some cleanup. This "cleanup" is the "pop-up-hide-finish-if-needed" algorithm.

The purpose of this line is to cancel the event listener on the animation, since we don't want to run pop-up-hide-finish-if-needed now that the popup is open again.

In my original draft for the spec, I tried to define the entire [PopupAnimationFinishedListener](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/dom/popup_animation_finished_event_listener.cc) class which looked really weird and took a ton of spec text. Mason suggested that I do it in one sentence kind of like this instead, which I see now isn't clear enough.

Do you have any ideas how to revise this? Maybe I could try to create a cancelable task to run pop-up-hide-finish-if-needed which gets run when the animations events are fired...?

Those are basically cases where the event handler *also* shows or hides the pop-up, which I can see happening often either on purpose or on accident. Since the pop-up was in a good enough state when the function was actually called (I.e. the initial checks passed), I don’t think it should throw exceptions **later** after the operation has already started. I can see that being frustrating and more confusing than helpful. But maybe I’m missing something?

body:
At least in Chromium, it's "bad":tm: to fire synchronous events when an element is being removed from the document. So I made it async in that case. It unfortunately uses the same flag for the case when the "hide immediately" behavior is due to another top-layer element being added, and it likely doesn't need to be async in that case.

See discussion here: https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/578#issuecomment-1270861298

I'm open to change this to something reasonable.

body:
Sure, you could have a complex event handler that shows and hides the pop-up, all from one call. The first call to `showPopUp()` triggers the `show` event, and the event handler calls `hidePopUp()`, which triggers `hide`, whose event handler calls `showPopUp()`. All of that would run before the first call to `showPopUp()` gets to the line we're discussing. Depending on animations, any one of those calls could either be complete (i.e. the pop-up is now fully showing/hidden) or transitioning (animating in or out). At the point where you call `showPopUp` things should be tractable for the developer, so throwing exceptions based on state feels right. But after events start firing, it feels unfortunate to throw exceptions based on things that technically happen "after" starting to show or hide.

Maybe I'm too concerned about this. I suppose we could throw exceptions in these cases and see who complains. But it feels like a developer could easily add event handlers that `console.log` the show/hide events and see what's going on with their code, if they're confused about why their pop-up silently didn't show up after a call, right?

State + Keywords + Description +
Auto state + auto + Closes other pop-ups when opened; has light + dismiss. +
The empty string +
Hint state + hint + Closes other hint pop-ups when opened; has light + dismiss. +
Manual state + manual + Does not close other pop-ups; does not light + dismiss. +
+ +

The popUp IDL attribute + must reflect the popup attribute.

+ +

The attribute may be omitted. The invalid value default + and the missing value default are both the manual state. + +

When the popup attribute is not set an an element, then the + element's popup attribute is considered to be in the no pop-up state.

+ +

Every element which has the popup attribute not in the no pop-up state has an additional pop-up visibility + state with these potential values:

+
    +

  • hidden

    • + +

  • transitioning

    • + +

  • showing

    • +
+ +
+

The pop-up visibility transitioning state and :open pseudo selectors exist to allow pop-ups to animate open or + closed because animating between display:none and other display values is not possible.

The following is an example of an animated pop-up:

+ + 
<div popup="auto" id="foo">
+  A fancy pop-up with no Javascript
+</div>
+<style>
+  [popup] {
+    opacity: 0;
+    transform: translate(-100px,100px);

      3. + +

    3. If ancestor is not null, then run hide + all pop-ups until with endpoint set to ancestor, focus previous element set + to false, hide immediately set to false, and hide unrelated set to true.

      4. +

  13. +

    If this's popup attribute is in the auto state, then run the following steps:

    + +
      +

    1. Let ancestor be the result of running the nearest open ancestral + pop-up algorithm with this and new pop-up.

      2. + +

    2. Run hide all pop-ups until with endpoint + set to ancestor, focus previous element set to false, hide immediately set to false, + and hide unrelated set to true.

      3. +

      +

      +

      +
      + +

      If this's popup attribute is in the no pop-up state, then return.

      +

    2. If this's pop-up visibility state is not hidden, then return.

      3. + +

    4. +

Ok, I replaced pop-up focusable area with focus delegate.

I have been working for a while on implementing code in chromium to pass dialog-focus-shadow.html and I posted about it in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/8174, which I assume is the same "focus delegate" thing. I'm not done with the chromium implementation yet, it was more complicated than I thought and requires webui changes to add delegatesfocus which hopefully the reviewer is ok with.

body:
I guess there could be two questions you're asking:
 - Why INT_MAX and not UINT_MAX or some other big number?
 - Why pick a big number?

I don't care about the answer to the first question, so if there's a better choice, pick it! If it's the second question, then the point of this code is to find the highest ("nearest") point in the stack that is an ancestor, and upper_bound keeps track of how high we can go without going "over" the provided element. We start with a big number so that in the case that we're looking for something that isn't in the pop-up stack, we include everything.

Not sure that answers your question.

body:
First, here's the part of the Anchor Positioning spec that (too implicitly, I think) refers to this `anchor` attribute: https://tabatkins.github.io/specs/css-anchor-position/#implicit-anchor-elements

As for the description, there are a couple editorial nits, but more importantly:
> If the other element's [popup](https://html.jarhar.com/multipage/pop-up.html#attr-popup) attribute is also not in the [no pop-up state](https://html.jarhar.com/multipage/pop-up.html#attr-popup-none-state), then the other element is considered to be a parent in the pop-up hierarchy.

Note that the "other element" doesn't have to itself be a pop-up. The other element could be a descendant of a pop-up. The existing "nearest open ancestral pop-up" algorithm should correctly find it in this case also.

I wonder if perhaps there could be a more general description (non-normative) of the ways that pop-ups can become related to one another, through DOM tree, invoking attributes, and the `anchor` attribute?

Ok, as I'm implementing this, I realize this would open a whole other set of cans of worms. The HidePopupInternal function can be called from a number of places, most of which *aren't* Javascript. For example, when a user clicks outside a pop-up and invokes light-dismiss, that calls HidePopupInternal on all of the pop-ups. If I change the cases we're talking about, those can now throw exceptions. Obviously they can't throw exceptions in that case, so I guess we'll just have to add spec language (and code) to explicitly ignore all of the exceptions in all of those cases. Feels ugly/wrong as I'm implementing it.

I'd like to revisit.

> Thanks, I removed the part saying that the parent needs to be a popup. I didn't know tab already wrote a css spec for anchor positioning. I suppose it still makes sense to define it here too, right...?

Yes, I definitely think it needs to be defined here, as an HTML attribute. You could perhaps *refer* to the spec though. Maybe. @domenic will have better input here.

> > I wonder if perhaps there could be a more general description (non-normative) of the ways that pop-ups can become related to one another, through DOM tree, invoking attributes, and the anchor attribute?

> Yeah this could be helpful as a note or something for the complicated algorithms like find nearest open ancestral pop-up. Maybe this is a good starting point...? https://open-ui.org/components/popup.research.explainer#nearest-open-ancestral-pop-up

Let's do this: I'll re-work that section a bit, and try to write a better "Note" type description of the rationale. And then you can copy/paste that to the spec, if it looks good. Sound ok?

The "canceling an animation" and "finishing an animation" concepts linked here are to the algorithms invoked from `animation.cancel()` and `animation.finish()`. Is the intention that this should be equivalent to `await Promise.all([animation.cancel(), animation.finish()])`?

I suspect not, and that what you need here is a condition you can await, perhaps https://drafts.csswg.org/web-animations-1/#play-state?

It looks like `element.popUp` cannot be null and this doesn't need to be nullable. That's because `popUp` is defined to reflect `popup`, and that's an enumerated attribute, it could only be one of the strings "auto", "hint" or "manual".

body: Defining the **no pop-up state** separately from the above table of states leads to a strange consequence. The missing value default is defined to be the **manual state**, but at the same time the attribute is considered to be in this no pop-up state. Scripts would see `element.popUp === 'manual'` and can't easily check if we're in the no pop-up state using the IDL attribute. It looks well defined, but I want to double check this is fully intentional?
Hmm, perhaps the intention is to use the "limited to only known values" qualifier for reflection? Without that we'll actually hit an assert in the spec currently.

Hmm, I think the difference is missing **value** vs. missing **attribute**. When the value is missing, it uses the missing value default, and gets `manual`. When the attribute is missing, the IDL attribute returns `null`. I believe scripts can therefore tell the difference, right?

body:
Alright, the new wording is "Wait for each animation in animations to fire either a cancel event or a finish event."

Waiting for events to fire seems to be rare in web specs, but not wrong. But you probably want to ensure the events are [trusted](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-event-istrusted), so that `animation.dispatchEvent(new Event('cancel'))` doesn't work.

If is another way to express the same wait condition I think that'd be slightly better. Would it be equivalent to wait until https://drafts.csswg.org/web-animations-1/#play-state is not "running"? That would add the paused state to the mix, not sure if that's good or bad?

If "limited to only known values" is added, then it can return null without hitting that assert.

body:
These are declared as `DOMString?`, but I think they should just be `DOMString`.

Below in their definitions, they [reflect](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#reflect) the appropriate content attributes. However, if you look at the section titled "If a reflecting IDL attribute has the type [DOMString](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#idl-DOMString)?", you will quickly hit an assert. The content attributes are not enumerated attributes, so the spec will crash.

---

However, it would be even better if we changed these to be of type `Element?`. That's generally the more modern style, which we designed as a generalization of `inputElement.list` and `formAssociatedElement.form`, and is being used for all the ARIA attributes.

> However, it would be even better if we changed these to be of type `Element?`. That's generally the more modern style, which we designed as a generalization of `inputElement.list` and `formAssociatedElement.form`, and is being used for all the ARIA attributes.

So we discussed this on https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/382#issuecomment-1184966802, and decided to wait on the `...Element` versions of this API. Since the content attribute is a `DOMString`, doesn't that require the reflected IDL to also be a string? I thought that was ironclad. Our plan had been to come back to the `...Element` versions of the content attribute and corresponding IDL later, once we establish that there's a need for it. Does that make sense?

> The content attribute is a string referencing an ID of another element. That means it's best done as an `Element?`.

But there are a host of issues with this, right? If you set the IDL to an element that has no `id`, what does `element.getAttribute()` return? What happens if the element you provide is in another shadow tree, so that the `id` can't be used? What happens if the element you provide has a duplicate `id` to something else that comes earlier in the DOM? What happens if the content attribute is set to a value that doesn't exist as an `id` in the DOM, what does the IDL reflect?

When we discussed this in OpenUI, it seemed natural to (eventually) have:

```javascript
invoker.popoverToggleTarget === 'idref';
invoker.popoverToggleTargetElement === myPopoverElement;
```

...with only the first one provided for now. We [thought](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/382#issuecomment-1184773425) that was the way [AOM was moving also](https://wicg.github.io/aom/aria-reflection-explainer.html#reflecting-element-references). Are we wrong about that?

body:
The spec is https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#reflect, scroll down to "If a reflecting IDL attribute attr has the type T?, where T is either [Element](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#interface-element) or an interface that inherits from [Element](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#interface-element), then:"

Good point about the element suffix. I think our original plan was to only include the suffix if there were both Element-based and string-based reflection, and omit them otherwise. But I guess that did not end up happening; ARIA only has element-based versions, and they all have suffixes.

That means there will be some minor inconsistency with existing non-ARIA cases like `list` and `form` (which we want to extend to be read/write and use the reflection infrastructure where possible). But oh well.

body:
Not quite... There are a number of issues here. If you were to use in parallel, you'd need to avoid manipulating main-thread state (e.g. "waiting to hide popover") or calling main-thread algorithms (e.g. "popover hide finish if needed") from the in-parallel thread. Instead you'd probably move the first step outside the parallel block, and queue a task to do the last step.

However, if this is event handler based, it sounds like waiting and in-parallel is maybe not the right infrastructure. Note my other comment about how using event listeners from specs/browser code is fraught: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/7785#issuecomment-1294296444

I'm not sure what the right path here is. In particular, I'd encourage you to look through https://drafts.csswg.org/web-animations-1/#finishing-an-animation-section and https://drafts.csswg.org/web-animations-1/#canceling-an-animation-section and determine exactly where this popover hiding logic should be inserted. Is it really correct that it should be exactly at the point where author code runs event handlers? Or maybe it should be after all the animation stuff is done, but before author code? Or maybe after author code? Maybe after the promise?

Ah I see, sorry I was looking at the wrong call to check popover validity.

> in 8.4 the popover attribute is explicitly checked for no changes relative to 8.1. So how can it have changed in 8.5 relative to step 5

"Check popover validity" looks at more than just than just the value of the popover attribute. If the script run by 8.3 calls showPopover on the element, then 8.5 will catch it but 8.4 won't. If script in 8.3 sets the element's popover attribute to "manual", then 8.4 will catch it but 8.5 won't.

This is the same thing that the chromium implementation does: https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/html_element.cc;l=1327-1329;drc=f65a43442f3e8e8d31bed5aa2f55c3fd68180da6

body:
Thanks for the spec pointer - that behavior looks very reasonable to me. I like how it side-steps the idref problem in the case that you set the IDL attribute.

So it sounds like you're ok with the Element reflections for this PR being `popover*TargetElement` (i.e. with `Element` suffix). Just confirming that. Do you see those as *required* now as part of this PR, or could we add them later? (The OpenUI [resolved](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/382#issuecomment-1184773425) to wait until later for those, to learn more about the use cases.)

body:
We can only reach this point of the first call to "check popover validity" succeeded and no exception was thrown. For both `showPopover()` and `hidePopover()` the current PR (squash and rebase 34) first does the check and throws exceptions if it fails, and does it again after events are fired, but if it fails just silently returns. There are 4 such call sites that just to "then return" but I only suggested it here.

For `hidePopover()` I think there's a good argument for silent return: if the event handler just removed the element, it's still hidden. The focus restoring logic won't run, but if that's a problem we can change the algorithm and make that work, while still not throwing an exception.

For `showPopover()` I don't understand the reason though. If the event handler does something that now makes it impossible to show the popover, the operation can't be finished, so isn't an exception appropriate?

I think this isn't cut and dry, it's a judgment call, but I don't quite get the reason for it.

body: As with the equivalent cases in `hidePopover()`, there are places that get called where an exception can't be thrown. For example, from [here](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/forms/html_form_control_element.cc;l=409;drc=a98d92c84d9821c8de97618095ed9df220cd1da7) (the case when an invoking element like a button triggers the popover). The general problem with all of these cases, which happen *after* an event handler runs, is that all of the state can be changed by the event handler. Before the event handler, it makes sense to throw exceptions, since the pre-conditions can be checked. After event handlers, that's not the case.

If I understand this suggestion, all that would be required is to split the existing hidePopover algorithm into two pieces, one before the event is fired and one after. And the former calls the latter. And then elsewhere (e.g. in the light dismiss routines) you only call the second one, which doesn't throw.

E.g.
```
hide popover 1:
 1. If error conditions, throw exception
 2. Fire hide event.
 3. Call hide popover 2.

hide popover 2:
 1. If error conditions, return.
 2. Do the rest...

light dismiss algorithm:
 1. If we want to light dismiss popover, call hide popover 2 with popover.
```

If we moved this check to "popover target element", then disabled buttons etc. could never count as openers when we look for them later. Consider the following: ```html
hello world 1
hello world 2
``` Clicking on `button1` will open `popover2` and disable itself. If "popover target element" doesn't consider `button1` anymore due to it being disabled, then `popover2` will no longer be considered a child of `popover1` according to "topmost popover ancestor" or "topmost clicked popover", and things like light dismiss won't work as expected - clicking on `popover2` might cause `popover1` to close.

body: We [discussed this at length in OpenUI](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/578) with the options considered being async event or no event. The fairly strong [consensus](https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/578#issuecomment-1334236879) among developers was that an async event was far better than no event, and it’s a corner case anyway to have the element removed from the document.

body:
In that discussion though the event had a different name. That's the whole point for raising this, because before this problem didn't exist.

Speaking of which, `beforetoggle` seems awfully generic for a feature named `popover`.

Maybe this would be acceptable:

* Normally we fire `beforepopovertoggle` events using the `BeforePopoverToggleEvent` event class.
* For this case we fire a `popoverhide` event using the `Event` event class.

body:
Regarding `beforetoggle`:
1. OpenUI decided to merge the `popoverhide` and `popovershow` events into one event here: https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/607#issuecomment-1319114654
2. Domenic suggested that we name it `beforetoggle` instead of `toggle` since it isn't async like the `<details>` element's `toggle` event.

> Speaking of which, beforetoggle seems awfully generic for a feature named popover.

I don't think the `toggle` event is fired for anything besides the details element, but in the interest of moving this PR along I am happy to rename the `beforetoggle` event to `beforepopovertoggle`.

> For this case we fire a popoverhide event using the Event event class.

I think it would be hard to explain a new unique event type for this corner case. I'd rather just not fire events at all. However, as mason said, developers at OpenUI said that an async event is better than no event.

What if we called it `popovertoggle`? This doesn't imply that the event comes before the actual toggling which resolves this issue, and doesn't run into the issue domenic pointed out which lead us to rename it from `toggle` to `beforetoggle` - which is that `toggle` is async for details elements. It also complies with the OpenUI resolution to use one event name for showing and hiding.

If the event needs to be different when its sync vs async, can we add an attribute to it to indicate whether its sync or async instead of giving it a different name? In the case where a developer wants to keep track of state change but doesn't care about it being sync vs async, having to listen to two different event types doesn't seem great.

body: So we discussed this (async event for the corner case where the element is removed from the document) at OpenUI with a room full of developers. It was a total non-issue to anyone there. The preference was to still fire the event in this case, but barely. This seems to be a spec-only problem, not one that actually impacts developers. Maybe shouldn’t be inventing whole new events and event classes just for this corner case?

> There's another problem here, these events fire with cancelable false yet expect being cancelable? (Although the queued event isn't cancelable of course.)

I set cancelable to true or false accordingly, thanks for catching that

> Also, perhaps we should expose the state on the element instead and not through the event? Seems somewhat nicer if people don't have to do bookkeeping for it. E.g., popoverVisibility that returns "hidden" or "shown". (The current prose uses "showing", but isn't "shown" the opposite of "hidden"?)

If we moved the state from the event to the element then an async hiding beforetoggle would look the same as an opening beforetoggle, right?

The only other way I can think of resolving this is to run the entire popover hiding algorithm from a task when we aren't allowed to fire an event. This would make things a lot more complicated though, since we would then be allowing funny states like the popover still being open but soon to be hidden when the popover attribute is removed - which is one of the places where we hide the popover with an async hiding event.

I believe Mason's last comment is the best way to go.

body:
I think `popovertoggle` with only `newState` is potentially acceptable. I think the resulting design is quite bad, but I think ultimately we need to decide by putting the event through some real-world demo code.

In particular the strange semantics I'm concerned about are:

- This event sometimes fires when the element is in the DOM, and sometimes when it isn't.
- This event sometimes has newState === the current state, and sometimes has newState === not the current state.

I think it would be better design from a theoretical perspective to have two events (e.g. `popoverremoved` and `beforepopovertoggle`, or something). But if you have a series of demos showing how two events would be more awkward than one, and that the above strange semantics don't cause problems, and that it's important for those demos that the event be sometimes sync and sometimes async (i.e., the demos would be worse if it was always async), then I'd be convinced.

Maybe updating the old Edge `<popup>` demos page would work?

I created a demo which as far as I can tell is not affected by the async hiding here: https://jsfiddle.net/jarhar/tynzfusw/
You can trigger async hiding by clicking the button to disconnect the popover from the document.

> e.g. popoverremoved and beforepopovertoggle

> This event sometimes fires when the element is in the DOM, and sometimes when it isn't.

It only now occurred to me that the *only* time that we do async events is when the popover is removed from the document while open. I previously thought that this also happened when the popover attribute is removed, but this is not the case.

With this in mind, maybe it does make sense to not fire any events at all when it is disconnected, as you alluded to about firing events on elements which aren't in the DOM. This appears to be the case for both [the details element](https://jsfiddle.net/jarhar/xgk7pe2n/) and [the dialog element](https://jsfiddle.net/jarhar/bzmdwxje/).

I don't have any context on whether firing events when opened popovers are disconnected is essential to any use cases though.

body:
> We definitely agree that we need to reach consensus here in WHATWG! But hopefully the input and careful discourse among the developers in OpenUI should be treated as an information-rich input to this consensus process, right?

For sure!

> So we have a number of demos that use popover, including all of the ones in the [blog post](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/pop-ups-theyre-making-a-resurgence/) (raw example code [here](https://codepen.io/collection/NqjRNE)), and the [<selectmenu> demo page](https://microsoftedge.github.io/Demos/selectmenu/) which uses popovers. None of these demos seem to be affected by the corner case we're discussing here, where an open popover is removed from the DOM.

Interesting! So does that mean we can go with one of the more coherent options then, since none of the demos rely on the less-coherent semantics? That is, either:

- Stop firing the event when the element is removed from the DOM; or
- Fire the event async always.

I think that might be what you mean by "the conclusion being that as long as the developer can correctly deduce the situation within the event handler, the async event is ok", but I'm not sure.

> That is, either:
> 
> * Stop firing the event when the element is removed from the DOM; or
> * Fire the event async always.
> 
> I think that might be what you mean by "the conclusion being that as long as the developer can correctly deduce the situation within the event handler, the async event is ok", but I'm not sure.

Of the two, I definitely think not firing the event is preferable to always being async. The only issue that raises is that to deal with the corner case, a Mutation Observer on the parent element would need to be used to watch for removals. Which is kind of a pain. We actually discussed this at yesterday’s OpenUI meeting and there was a (separate) desire to have a way to observe DOM removals on the element itself, rather than having to track the parent or document. Do you know of any prior requests for this functionality?

Regardless of that, and assuming this is the last issue we need to resolve in order to land this PR, I’m ok if we change the behavior to not fire the `beforetoggle` event at all in the case that the element is removed from the DOM. Sound good?

> > Of the two, I definitely think not firing the event is preferable to always being async.
> 
> OK. But there are no demos in existence currently that depend on the event being fired sync? Is that correct? I just want to confirm we are on the same page.

I believe that's correct, yes. Most of the demos are intended to show how much you can do declaratively, without JS.


> > We actually discussed this at yesterday’s OpenUI meeting and there was a (separate) desire to have a way to observe DOM removals on the element itself, rather than having to track the parent or document. Do you know of any prior requests for this functionality?
> 
> [whatwg/dom#533](https://github.com/whatwg/dom/issues/533)

Cool, thanks. I'll feed that back to the folks asking for it.


> > Regardless of that, and assuming this is the last issue we need to resolve in order to land this PR, I’m ok if we change the behavior to not fire the beforetoggle event at all in the case that the element is removed from the DOM. Sound good?
> 
> That would work for me. But I would still appreciate some clarity on where the sync requirement is coming from, if none of the demos are affected by sync vs. async.

So there are two big use cases that would be broken by async:
 1. popover content setup. You'd like to be able to add content to the popover before it shows.
 2. animations. You'd like to be able to set up animations that apply to the showing/hiding transition.

Even though we don't have demos for those cases, they definitely both came up often as concrete needs.
